name: Bredt's Rule
statement: A carbon-carbon double bond cannot form at the bridgehead of a small bridged bicyclic ring system without prohibitive strain.
statementAccent: at the bridgehead of a small bridged bicyclic ring system
meaning: Bredt's rule states that a bridgehead atom of a bridged ring system cannot normally be part of a carbon-carbon double bond, because such a double bond would have to be trans in at least one of the rings. In small ring systems this forces severe geometric distortion. Compounds that violate it are called anti-Bredt olefins.
mechanism: A double bond requires its two carbons and their substituents to be roughly coplanar with aligned p-orbitals for pi overlap. At the bridgehead of a small bicyclic framework, the rigid ring geometry cannot accommodate this without large ring strain and angle strain, destabilizing or preventing the alkene. Stability improves as the rings grow larger.

examples.text: Bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-1-ene (1-norbornene) is a classic anti-Bredt olefin, so strained that it is highly reactive and not isolable under ordinary conditions.
Bredt derived the rule from failed attempts to place double bonds at bridgeheads in camphane- and pinane-type bicyclic terpene derivatives.
Anti-Bredt alkenes become isolable when the ring system is large enough, and recent work has trapped strained anti-Bredt olefins as reactive intermediates.

whyItMatters: The rule guides synthetic chemists in judging whether a target bridgehead alkene is feasible and in avoiding structures that will not form. It sharpened understanding of how ring strain and orbital geometry govern which pi bonds are attainable.
limits: It is a guideline tied to ring size, not an absolute prohibition: sufficiently large bridged systems tolerate bridgehead double bonds. It also does not straightforwardly apply to formal double bonds drawn on hypervalent heteroatoms.
misreadings: "Impossible" overstates it; anti-Bredt alkenes exist but are strained and reactive, and the cutoff depends on ring size rather than being a hard ban.
origin: Julius Bredt, German chemist (1855–1937), discussed the idea in 1902 and formalized the rule in 1924.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on Bredt's rule, stating a bridgehead double bond must be trans in at least one ring and is strained in small systems — supports the statement, mechanism, and limits.
Wikipedia's biography of Julius Bredt, confirming his dates and that he proposed in 1924 that a double bond cannot sit at the bridgehead of a bridged ring — supports the attribution and date.
